title: Water all through it
hook: rain, springs, rivers of the garden: water as mercy all through the book

segments.voice: Yesterday, signs in nature, and your line: the world is signs. What did you read slowly, an ant, a tree, a cloud? Today, one sign that runs through the whole book like a river. Day six hundred seventy.

Turn on a tap. It's the most forgettable act of the day: brushing teeth, filling a kettle, rinsing a cup. Now imagine hearing the Qur'an for the first time in the Hijaz, where a well could decide whether a town existed, and a caravan's route was drawn from one water source to the next. In that place, water isn't background. It's life and death. No surprise, then, that it flows through the book from its first pages to its last pictures of the Garden.
screen: `A LAND WHERE A WELL MAKES A TOWN.`

segments.voice: Start at the beginning of things. Surah twenty-one says Allah made every living thing from water. Surah eleven pictures His throne upon the water before the heavens and earth were made. Then the rain. Surah seven describes the winds sent ahead as good news, going before His mercy, and that mercy is the rain: clouds driven to a dead land, and out of it every kind of fruit. Rain is so often paired with mercy that in many places the two almost share a sentence. Springs burst from rock when Musa strikes it with his staff, twelve of them, one for each tribe. And at the far end of the book, the Garden is again and again called gardens beneath which rivers flow. Surah forty-seven names rivers of water that never goes stale. Water is in the daily life of the faith too. No prayer without washing first, the wudu: hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head, feet. And here's a detail that surprises people. A hadith in al-Bukhari says the Prophet ﷺ would do his whole wudu with about one mudd of water, roughly two cupped handfuls, and bathe with a few times that. Another hadith, in Abu Dawud, says people are partners in three things: water, pasture and fire. So water in Islamic teaching is a mercy from above, a trust held in common, and something not to be poured away. The same book that promises rivers asks you to use a handful well.

The practice: don't waste a drop today. Start here. If you have a glass of water, hold it. If not, picture one. Look at it before you drink. Think of where it came from: a cloud, a river, a reservoir, a pipe someone laid. Then drink slowly, in small sips, with a breath between each, until it's gone or you've had enough. If you'd like, many Muslims begin with bismillah and finish with alhamdulillah. Notice that you didn't spill any. The bell holds the time.
Water all through it. From every living thing made of water, through rain as mercy, to rivers beneath the Garden, and a wudu from two handfuls. Today's word.
Your line: water is mercy. Today, turn off one tap sooner than you usually would, while brushing, washing, or waiting for it to warm. Day six hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Muslims wash with water (wudu) before every prayer and try to use little of it, following hadith about the Prophet's small measure; many say bismillah before drinking and alhamdulillah after.

fork.reveal: the Prophet did his wudu with about one mudd of water, a small measure even in a land of wells.

trapdoor: what you thought: water shows up now and then in religious stories.
what it means: water runs through the Qur'an as mercy: life made from it, rain before mercy, rivers in the Garden.
what a scholar hears: the hadith of the mudd (about two handfuls for wudu) and of people as partners in water shaped Islamic law on water as shared and not to be wasted.
